456.title: If He took the ten
456.hook: what could the ungrateful say if the ten were taken too
456.howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza in Sukhmani Sahib, and many describe gratitude to Waheguru as part of everyday remembrance rather than a separate ritual.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten things and one: ten gifts put behind the back, and trust thrown away over the one. Your line was ten given, one held back. Today the same stanza asks a sharp question. Day four hundred fifty-six.

Picture the birthday table again. The child is sulking over the eleventh present. Now imagine the table empty. Not ten and a missing one. Nothing. No cake, no wrapping paper, no party. What would there be to complain about then? Who would there be to complain to? It's a question that stops a sulk in its tracks, and it isn't asked to frighten anyone. It's asked to turn the head around. Guru Arjan asks it in the very next line of the stanza, and then, surprisingly, he doesn't leave us standing in front of the empty table.
screen: `NOW IMAGINE THE TABLE EMPTY.` → `WHO WOULD YOU COMPLAIN TO?` → `A QUESTION THAT TURNS THE HEAD.`

segments.voice: The line goes: ek bhee na dei, das bhee hir lei. If He gave not even the one, and took back the ten as well. Then: tau moorhaa kahu kahaa karei. Then tell me, what could the fool do? Moorhaa is a blunt word: the foolish one, the one not thinking. The answer is in the silence after the question. Nothing. There's no court to appeal to, no account to draw on. Everything on the table came from the same hands. So the stanza goes on: jis thaakur sio naahee chaaraa. With the Master before whom we have no leverage, no say. Taa kau keejai sad namaskaaraa: to Him, bow, always. That could sound like fear. Bow, because you have no choice. But listen to the next line, because it changes the whole stanza. Jaa kai man laagaa prabh meethaa: in whose mind God has come to taste sweet. Sarab sookh taahoo man voothaa: every comfort comes to live in that mind. Meethaa is the word for sweet, the taste of sugar on the tongue. So the sum turns into something else. The person who sees the ten and thanks for them isn't cornered into bowing. They've started to like the Giver. And gratitude, for them, stops being a duty and becomes a taste. That's the move: from the empty table, to the full one, to the hands that set it.
screen: `IF HE TOOK THE TEN AS WELL.` · `WHAT COULD THE FOOL DO?` · `BOW TO THE MASTER, ALWAYS.` · `MEETHAA: GOD TASTES SWEET.` · then, large: `THANK FOR THE TEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: be grateful for one small thing. Not the big ones. Something tiny. The warmth of the cup in your hand. A sock without a hole. The light coming in from one window. Pick one, and stay with it. Notice it as if, for a moment, it had been taken away and then handed back. If you pray, you can thank the Giver for it in your own way. If you don't, just let yourself be glad of it, slowly, the way you'd let something sweet sit on your tongue. The bell holds the time.
If He took the ten. Ek bhee na dei, das bhee hir lei: if not even one were given, and the ten taken too, what could anyone do?
screen: `IF HE TOOK THE TEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: thank for the ten. Today, before you name what's missing, name one thing on the table, out loud or in your head. Day four hundred fifty-six.

457.title: Living ashtpadi 5
457.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of all they have as Waheguru's gift held in trust, and gratitude is part of daily remembrance, including in the Ardas, which gives thanks before it asks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, if He took the ten: the empty table, and the mind where God tastes sweet. Your line was thank for the ten. Today, we live ashtpadi five, with one more picture from it. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

In old Punjab, a village moneylender, a saahu, might hand a trader capital to work with. The trader buys, sells, eats well, throws a wedding. Years pass. He starts to think of the money as his own. Then one day the saahu asks for some of it back. Not all. Some. And the trader is furious, as though he's being robbed. Everyone in the village can see what's happened. Everyone except the trader. The second stanza of ashtpadi five tells that story, and it's the clearest picture yet of what gratitude is for.
screen: `THE SAAHU LENDS HIS CAPITAL.` → `YEARS PASS; IT FEELS LIKE MINE.` → `ASKED FOR SOME, HE'S FURIOUS.`

segments.voice: Guru Arjan tells it plainly. The banker gives his capital. The man eats and drinks and lives in delight. Then the banker takes back a little of what was only ever held in trust, and the ignorant one rages. By his anger he loses his own credit. Nobody will trust him with anything again. Then the turn: the wise one places what belongs to the owner back before the owner, and accepts the order with his forehead bowed. And the stanza says that person is made happy four times over. Put that next to the last three days. The salok named God the Giver. The ten things showed how gifts slip behind our backs. The empty table asked what we'd say if they were all gone. Now the banker shows the long game. Gratitude isn't only a nice feeling. It's how you stay trustworthy with what you've been lent. The trader who forgot it was a loan is the one who couldn't let any of it go. And everything goes, in the end: health, strength, time, people we love. Sikh teaching doesn't pretend otherwise. What it offers is a way of holding all of it now, as a trust, so that when some of it is called back, the hands are already open. That's why gratitude is the practice of this ashtpadi. Not a mood. A habit of counting, so the ten never fall behind the back.
screen: `THE BANKER LENDS; THE MAN FEASTS.` · `ASKED FOR SOME, HE RAGES.` · `PUT IT BACK BEFORE THE OWNER.` · `GRATITUDE KEEPS THE HANDS OPEN.` · then, large: `COUNT THE TEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: list ten gifts. If you have paper or a notes app, write them down; otherwise say them quietly. This time, choose ten you'd feel the loss of: someone's voice, your hands, a friend who still calls, a skill you learned, a place that feels like home. Write each one, and after it, the word: lent. Not to make you sad. Just to see them as the stanza sees them. When you have ten, put the list down, close your eyes, and breathe with all ten held lightly. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi five. Its practice is gratitude: seeing what we have as the banker's capital, lent and not owned.
Your line: count the ten. Keep today's list somewhere you'll see it tonight, and read it once before sleep. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

screen: `DAY 457 COUNTS.` → `ASHTPADI 5, LIVED.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 6, SALOK: THE THIEVES LEAVE.`

458.title: Ashtpadi 6, salok: the thieves leave
458.hook: lust, anger, greed and attachment go, and pride too, by grace
458.howItsDone: Sikhs name kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankaar as the five thieves, and in Sukhmani Sahib and the Ardas they ask for the Guru's grace and protection against them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi five: the banker's capital, and a list of ten gifts. Your line was count the ten. Is the list still where you left it? Today, ashtpadi six begins. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

You may remember them from last year: the five thieves. Kaam, lust. Krodh, anger. Lobh, greed. Moh, attachment. Ahankaar, pride. The Guru Granth Sahib pictures them living inside the house of the body, quietly carrying off whatever is valuable. Last year we met them as a list. You probably also met them in your own life this week, maybe more than once. Ashtpadi six opens by naming them again, all five, in a single line. But this time the salok isn't describing the thieves. It's asking for something. And what it asks for is the surprise.
screen: `THE FIVE THIEVES, AGAIN.` → `LIVING IN THE HOUSE OF THE BODY.` → `THIS TIME, THE SALOK ASKS.`

segments.voice: The salok's first line lists them: kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, and then ahanmev, which is pride, the sense of I alone, I myself. And it asks that they be destroyed, that they go. You might expect the second line to give a method. Five steps. A discipline for each thief. Instead the second line says: Nanak has come to God's sanctuary; bless me with Your grace, O divine Guru. The word for sanctuary is saranaagatee, coming for refuge, the way someone runs to a protected house when they're being chased. The word for grace is prasaad, a gift freely given. So the salok's answer to the five thieves isn't a fight in the dark. It's a door, and a request. Run to the house that's safe, and ask. That doesn't mean Sikhs sit back and do nothing. Elsewhere the Gurus speak of effort, of discipline, of living a disciplined, honest life, and the Sikh path is full of it. But this salok says something about where the change finally comes from. Pride can't be beaten by more pride, even pride in being humble. Anger can't be shouted down. The house is cleared by grace, coming in from outside. And that sets up the whole of ashtpadi six. Over the next three days it's going to repeat one phrase again and again: jih prasaad. By whose grace. The salok has just introduced the word.
screen: `LUST, ANGER, GREED, ATTACHMENT, PRIDE.` · `SARANAAGATEE: RUN FOR REFUGE.` · `PRASAAD: A GIFT FREELY GIVEN.` · `CLEARED FROM OUTSIDE, NOT FOUGHT.` · then, large: `GRACE CLEARS THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: breathe out one thief. Sit comfortably. Without judging yourself, let one of the five come to mind, the one that visited most this week. Lust, anger, greed, clinging, or pride. Just name it. Then breathe in slowly, as if the door of the house were opening. And as you breathe out, picture that thief walking out through it. You're not chasing it. You're making room. If you pray, you can ask for grace in your own way. Breathe in: open door. Breathe out: one thief leaves. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi six. Its salok names the five thieves, and asks for grace, prasaad, from the sanctuary of the Guru.
Your line: grace clears the house. Today, when one of the five shows up, don't wrestle it. Open a door: step outside, drink water, breathe once. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: the thieves leave when you try hard enough.

459.title: By whose grace
459.hook: jih prasaad: by whose grace you eat fine foods and wear fine clothes, remember Him
459.howItsDone: Many Sikhs remember Waheguru before eating, and in the gurdwara karah prashad is received in cupped hands as a gift of grace; ashtpadi six's 'jih prasaad' refrain is read as part of Sukhmani Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sixth salok: five thieves, and a request for grace. Your line was grace clears the house. Today, that word grace becomes a drumbeat. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

Jih prasaad. Jih prasaad. Jih prasaad. Read ashtpadi six aloud and those two words come round again and again, at the start of line after line, like a drum keeping time under a song. By whose grace. By whose grace. By whose grace. Each time, a different gift follows. And the gifts in the first stanza are surprisingly ordinary for a sacred text. Not visions. Not miracles. Dinner. Perfume. A comfortable house. A good shirt. The things you used today without a second thought.
screen: `JIH PRASAAD, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `A DRUM UNDER THE SONG.` → `DINNER, PERFUME, A GOOD SHIRT.`

segments.voice: Jih means by whom, by whose. Prasaad, you met yesterday: grace, a gift freely given. In the gurdwara, the sweet offering handed to everyone at the end of a service is called karah prashad, from the same family of words, given into cupped hands. So jih prasaad: by whose free gift. The first stanza goes like this. By whose grace you eat the thirty-six delicacies, an old Indian way of saying every kind of fine food, keep that Master in your mind. By whose grace you put fragrance on your body, remembering Him you reach the highest state. By whose grace you live in a house of comfort, meditate on Him always. And the next stanza picks up the clothes: by whose grace you wear silks and fine cloth, why abandon Him and cling to another? Notice the pattern. Every line has two halves. The first half is a gift you can taste, smell, touch. The second half is a turning: remember, keep in mind, don't forget. Guru Arjan doesn't ask anyone to give up the meal or the shirt. He asks for the meal to become a reminder. The food is real; it's where your attention goes next that the stanza cares about. It's the same move as the ten things, made smaller and more frequent. Not once a year at a feast. Every time you sit down to eat.
screen: `JIH: BY WHOSE. PRASAAD: FREE GIFT.` · `THE THIRTY-SIX DELICACIES.` · `EACH GIFT, THEN A TURNING.` · `THE MEAL BECOMES A REMINDER.` · then, large: `BY HIS GRACE, THIS MEAL.`

segments.voice: The practice is for your next meal: before you eat, pause and thank grace. For now, rehearse it. Picture the next thing you'll eat, a plate, a sandwich, a cup of tea. See where it came from: a field, a farmer, a truck, a shop, someone's hands. Then hear the drumbeat: jih prasaad, by whose grace. If you pray, let that be your thanks. If you don't, let it be a moment of noticing that none of it began with you. Breathe in: the meal. Breathe out: by whose grace. The bell holds the time.
By whose grace. Jih prasaad: the refrain of ashtpadi six, set before every ordinary gift.
Your line: by his grace, this meal. Before each meal today, even a snack, say the line once, silently, before the first bite. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 459 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BY WHOSE GRACE, THE BODY.`

460.title: By whose grace, the body
460.hook: by His grace you have a healthy body and a home
460.howItsDone: Sikhs read the 'jih prasaad' stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as reminders that health, home and family are gifts, and many share what they have through langar and seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by whose grace: the drumbeat over dinner and a good shirt. Your line was by his grace, this meal. Did you remember it at a meal? Today the same two words come closer to home. Day four hundred sixty.

Most of us only notice our bodies when something goes wrong. A sprained ankle, and suddenly every step is a project. A cold, and you'd give anything for one clear breath through the nose. Then it heals, and within a week you've forgotten again. The same with home: you notice the roof the night it leaks. Ashtpadi six keeps repeating jih prasaad, by whose grace, and in its later stanzas it turns from the plate and the wardrobe to the two things we forget most completely: the body we live in, and the house that holds it.
screen: `NOTICED ONLY WHEN IT HURTS.` → `THE ROOF, THE NIGHT IT LEAKS.` → `BY WHOSE GRACE: BODY AND HOME.`

segments.voice: One line says: jih prasaad aarog kanchan dehee. By whose grace you have a healthy, golden body. Aarog is health, being free of illness. Kanchan is gold. Dehee is the body. A golden body isn't about looks. In the old poetry, gold is what's precious and doesn't tarnish. So: by whose grace this precious, working body is yours. The second half, as always, turns: attune yourself to that loving Lord. And the same ashtpadi has already spoken of the house: by whose grace you live in a mansion of comfort, by whose grace you dwell at peace with your family. Another line even says, by whose grace your honor is kept covered, the things you'd rather nobody saw, quietly protected. Put those together and you get a picture of an ordinary good day: you woke up, you could move, nobody embarrassed you, there was a door to close behind you and people inside it. The stanza says none of that is automatic. Each is a jih prasaad. This doesn't mean anyone who is ill, or without a home, has lost grace. Gurbani speaks of rich and poor, healthy and sick, as living within the same hukam, and Sikhs are asked to share what they have, which is why the langar, the gurdwara kitchen, serves a free meal to anyone who comes in. The stanza is speaking to the one who has these things and forgets them, and it asks that person to notice.
screen: `AAROG: HEALTH. KANCHAN: GOLD.` · `DEHEE: THE BODY.` · `A HOUSE, A FAMILY, HONOR KEPT.` · `NOT AUTOMATIC: EACH A GIFT.` · then, large: `BY HIS GRACE, THIS HOME.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank your body and your home. Sit still. Start at your feet: they carried you today. Your hands: they held things. Your lungs: breathing, all by themselves. Whatever hurts, let it be there too; you're not pretending. Then widen out to the room around you, the walls, the roof, whoever shares this home with you, or the quiet if no one does. If you pray, you can give thanks with the words jih prasaad. If you don't, let each part simply be noticed and valued. The bell holds the time.
By whose grace. Today, jih prasaad aarog kanchan dehee: by whose grace a healthy, precious body, and a home to live in.
Your line: by his grace, this home. When you walk through your front door today, touch the frame, and say the line once. Day four hundred sixty.

461.title: Living ashtpadi 6
461.hook: every comfort points back to a Giver
461.howItsDone: In everyday Punjabi speech many Sikhs credit good news to 'Waheguru di kirpa', Waheguru's grace, while also thanking the people involved; ashtpadi six gives that habit its scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by whose grace, the body: a healthy body, a house, honor kept covered. Your line was by his grace, this home. Did you touch the door frame? Today we live ashtpadi six. Day four hundred sixty-one.

Ask a Punjabi grandmother how she is, and there's a good chance the answer starts with a small phrase before any news: Waheguru di kirpa naal. By Waheguru's grace. The harvest was good, by grace. The grandson passed his exams, by grace. The knee is better, by grace. It can sound like a habit of speech, and partly it is. But habits of speech are where a teaching goes to live. Sukhmani's sixth ashtpadi beats its drum, jih prasaad, for eight stanzas. In homes like hers, the drum never stopped.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU? BY GRACE.` → `A HABIT OF SPEECH.` → `WHERE A TEACHING GOES TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Kirpaa is another word for grace, kindness, favor. In ashtpadi four you met it in the child's prayer: in Your kirpaa are countless comforts. Ashtpadi six took that one line and spread it across a whole life: food, scent, clothes, house, family, health, honor. Every comfort, a gift. What does it look like to live that, not just read it? Try this. Take one comfort, a hot cup of tea. Trace it back. Someone boiled the water, maybe you. The water came through pipes someone laid, from rain that fell on hills you'll never see. The leaves were picked by hands, probably in Assam or Kenya or Sri Lanka, by people who got up before dawn. The milk came from an animal someone cared for. The warmth came from fire, or a power line, or the sun. Go back far enough and every comfort runs out of human causes and arrives at something none of us made. That's where Sikh teaching places the Giver: not instead of the farmer and the plumber, but behind and through all of them. Living ashtpadi six means two things at once. Thanks to the people, real thanks, by name if you can. And beneath that, the drumbeat: jih prasaad. By whose grace any of it exists at all. The grandmother's phrase holds both. The harvest was good because people worked. And by grace.
screen: `KIRPAA: GRACE, KINDNESS, FAVOR.` · `ONE CUP OF TEA, TRACED BACK.` · `PAST THE PEOPLE, TO THE GIVER.` · `THANKS TO BOTH, AT ONCE.` · then, large: `EVERY COMFORT A GIFT.`

segments.voice: The practice: trace one comfort to its source. Choose something you're touching or using right now: the chair, your clothes, the light, the device in your hand. Ask where it came from, and then where that came from. Name the people you pass on the way, even if only as the ones who made it, the ones who carried it. Keep going until you run out of people. Rest there, at the edge of what anyone made. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or simply sit there grateful. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi six. Every comfort points back, through many hands, to a Giver: jih prasaad, by whose grace.
Your line: every comfort a gift. Today, thank one person by name for one comfort you usually take for granted, and let the thanks keep going past them. Day four hundred sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 461 COUNTS.` → `ASHTPADI 6, LIVED.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 7, SALOK: THE HOLY COMPANY.`

trapdoor: what you thought: 'by grace' is just a figure of speech.
what it means: it's ashtpadi six lived out: every comfort points back to a Giver.
what a scholar hears: kirpaa (from Sanskrit kripaa) and prasaad are near-synonyms in Gurbani, alongside nadar and karam, the Granth's other words for grace.

462.title: Ashtpadi 7, salok: the holy company
462.hook: the salok praises the company of the holy
462.howItsDone: Sikhs gather as sangat, the congregation, in the gurdwara to sing and hear the Guru's word and to eat together in langar; ashtpadi seven of Sukhmani Sahib praises that holy company.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi six: one cup of tea, traced back past every hand to the Giver. Your line was every comfort a gift. Today, a new stretch of Sukhmani begins, ashtpadis seven to twelve. Day four hundred sixty-two, the end of a week.

Think of someone who, when they walk into a room, makes it a little easier to be good. You don't feel judged around them. You just find yourself speaking more kindly, complaining less, laughing more honestly. You leave them and notice you've been a better version of yourself for an hour, without trying. Almost everyone has met at least one person like that. For six ashtpadis, Sukhmani has been talking about the Giver and the gifts. Now, in the seventh, it turns to people: the holy, and what happens to us in their company.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO MAKES GOOD EASIER.` → `NOT JUDGED, JUST BETTER.` → `NOW SUKHMANI TURNS TO PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The salok has four short lines. First: the Supreme Lord is agam, out of reach, and agaadh, unfathomable, too deep to sound. Second: whoever speaks of Him is set free. Third: listen, friend, Nanak prays. And fourth: saadh janaa kee acharaj kathaa. The story of the holy ones is wondrous. Saadh, or saadhoo, is a holy person, someone whose life has been shaped by the Name. Acharaj is wonder, the feeling of seeing something you didn't think was possible. Notice the order. The salok starts with God beyond reach, and ends with people you can actually sit beside. That's the bridge this ashtpadi builds. The One who is too deep to sound becomes nearer in the company of those who remember Him. In Sikh life this has a very concrete shape: the sangat, the congregation, sitting together in the gurdwara, singing, eating side by side in the langar. Over the next days, the ashtpadi will list, line after line, what happens in that company. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago, ten things and one. Then, if He took the ten, and the mind where God tastes sweet. The banker's capital, lent, not owned. The five thieves and grace that clears the house. Jih prasaad over dinner, over the body and the home. Every comfort a gift. A week of the Giver. Now, the Giver's people.
screen: `AGAM, AGAADH: BEYOND REACH.` · `LISTEN, FRIEND, NANAK PRAYS.` · `ACHARAJ: THE WONDROUS STORY.` · `GOD FAR, THE HOLY NEAR.` · then, large: `GOOD COMPANY.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of your best company. Settle. Bring to mind one person in whose presence you become a little better. A grandparent, a teacher, a friend, someone you sat beside once and never forgot. Picture their face. Remember one thing they said, or the way they listened. Notice what happens in your body as you remember them: maybe the shoulders soften, maybe the jaw unclenches. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. Breathe in their company. Breathe out whatever you don't need to carry. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi seven. Its salok calls God beyond reach, and the story of the holy ones wondrous: acharaj.
Your line: good company. Today, send a short message to the person you pictured, and tell them, simply, that you thought of them. Day four hundred sixty-two. A week, done.
